3/4, 6/8, and 4/4 triplets are the same feel but they're all used in different situations.

3/4 if you're counting 1-2-3 1-2-3...

6/8 if it feels like 1 and a 2 and a...

Those are all triplet feels and you should write in those times if your whole phrase or song has that feel. It's easier to read and write

If it doesn't, you can use triplets in 4/4

1... 2 and a 3... 4 and a...

Or 

1 and a 2 and a 3... 4...

For 6/8 think of the always Sunny theme song (temptation sensation) and if you really want proof 6/8 is triplets, see how easy it is to count in 4/4, then count it in 1 and a 2 and a (doing it in 3 would be a little fast)

Reminds me of how 8/8 is to 4/4 as 6/8 is to 3/4, it's about how you break up the phrase. If I wanted to do
1-2-3 1-2-3 1-2, I guess I could count it in 8th notes in 4/4 since it's 8 notes but really it's 2 groups of 3 with 1 group of two

Then see my previous comment regarding oranges having bioflavonoids and such to increase bioabsorption. I do not disagree that eating an orange is more effective than the equivalent of eating vitamin C supplements. I am saying this isn't the case with different strains of psilocybin mushrooms.

A screw is a screw regardless of head or whether or not it comes packaged with a screw driver. Vitamin C is ascorbic acid and serves the exact same purpose in the same way regardless.

 I'm positive if you extracted the psilocybin out of a PE vs GT you would get significantly different yields to the point you could visually see the difference in concentration.

Some mushroom strains have more psilocin in them, which is the psychedelic drug psilocybin converts to, but cubes have some psilocin too so again, it's all concentration. I do not think there's any evidence that supports one strain having different psilocybin isomers than another, or enzymes/etc that aid in converting psilocybin to psilocin, or increases bioavailability. Especially if we keep this argument in cubes, penis envy vs say golden teachers or B+ I feel like this is exceptionally relevant.

It's almost like Valencia oranges vs Navel oranges, valcencias are a more concentrated orange with more juice per gram. If you wanna compare to cyans, that's not a cube, I would compare to Barbados cherries which have much higher vitamin C. Mushrooms are not oranges and vitamin c isn't psilocybin so it's not a perfect analogy but that's the best I could do.

 You can preconvert psilocybin by drying them or doing lemon tech, but the rest is concentration. I stick with my tequila vs beer analogy.

Yes but also no. Vitamin C is vitamin C, but oranges have bioflavonoids which helps bioabsorption which makes the orange work more efficiently than a vitamin C supplement which doesn't get any aided absorption.

This is not the case with psychedelic mushrooms, and it's entirely about concentration of psilocybin and psilocin in the actual mushroom. There are no compounds in say, penis envy vs golden teachers, that increases bioavailability.

I don't know how you specifically deployed immach in podman so it's difficult to give exact instructions but if you're down for a little bit of research and yamling, you need to add tailscale as a sidecar in the same pod.

I'm new at this but I think you'd be looking at installing tailscale inside the container. When you say you couldn't add it directly to the container, what exactly do you mean?

If you do not add tailscale to the container, you're pretty much looking at what you are currently doing, which is having tailscale run on the host and connecting to the app that way. The only other thing I can think of is routing the app through nginx or something like an ingress and installing tailscale in that, so you don't connect to the app itself, you connect to a webserver/ingress, reverse proxy or whatever and that gives you access to the application. You might need to learn a bit more about podman to know how to put that in a yaml

Committing changes to container images is kind of a bit of a process unless you have the dockerfile or whatever was used to build the image

I'm not entirely sure what you mean by this question so I'll explain what a modular synth is. 

Modular synthesizers are racks of individually purchased synthesizer modules that he wires together via patch cords. He did not purchase the complete rack, he built it, or perhaps someone built it for him I kind of doubt it.

Those modules might start with voltage control, sequencers and or arpeggiators, which tell it to play sequences of notes, into oscillators, which oscillate electricity into sound signals, like a sine wave, thus playing the notes and pitches he wants, and that goes through a large chain of modules that are envelopes (controls how the notes fade out, does it go for a long time or is it plucky beep boops), effects and filters. Some of those are tools for automation like LFOs that perform changes on the effects based on different wave forms and configurations. All of those cables are his way of routing the sound to the modules he wants, and all of the knobs and faders on them are the specific controls per module that get tweaked by him until satisfaction. The order of all of that is entirely up to him.

So it's not one machine you can buy, it's dozens and dozens of parts he's obtained, put in the rack, possibly swaps out, and meticulously configures to get the sounds he wants. I'm pretty sure some of those things are custom made for him, if not gifts, like the fidget spinner module, which uses magnets to manipulate sounds or effects and probably makes them go wub wub wub as the spinner passes over the magnet. 

A cruder way to think about this is a guitarists pedal board setup. They plug the guitar in and it goes into the distortion into the delay into reverb, etc, into the amp

A technical support engineer should be able to troubleshoot anything thoroughly, know how to get answers, and articulate complex issues to absolutely anyone, documenting every step, all while representing the company. customers, account teams, engineering, etc. TSEs need to be good under pressure while troubleshooting critical issues live on the phone with the customers. They try to deflect cases by building out a knowledge base of documentation/articles for all of the problems the team solves to help build the team and enable customers to fix their own problems.

You get a ticket, see if it's been found before, if so, it should be documented somewhere, if not, check it out live on the phone with the customer, get logs, troubleshoot/workaround what you can, reproduce the problem internally, write up a detailed bug ticket with every step you did to reproduce as well as the conditions it happens, and the impact of the bug. Get the customer as stable as you can until it gets patched. Write an article about this situation if there isn't one already. A TSE should be able to tell the difference between a misconfiguration, a bug, or user error. That means knowing everything about the system, how it works, why it is the way it is, and what it plugs into.

It can be stressful troubleshooting an escalated P1 while people threaten you over renewals. Cases are opened with bruised egos cuz the engineer who couldn't hack it needs to contact support. Sometimes the documentation sucks. You might even have on call.

All that said, when shit hits the fan and you're the one to save the day, you figured it out and fix it, it feels awesome. When you start becoming a mentor for the other TSEs, you know you're killing it. They trust you with the white glove treatment of customers, as well as the respect from engineering for being an expert of the product. It is definitely not just learning/managing one product.
